catalog_quote: Stress occurs on the first syllable regardless of weight, and on every syllable which surfaces with a long vowel (Rice 1992, 63-65). When morphological concatenation results in adjacent strings of syllables all of which have long vowels, the even numbered syllables in that string surface with a short vowel and no stress.. readall_conflicts: The one listed work could not be opened, so it cannot settle anything. Among the sources already held there is a known disagreement: WALS (feature 15A, source Geytenbeek & Geytenbeek 1971) codes Gidabal as fixed initial stress with no weight sensitivity, whereas the StressTyp2 entry for this language (Rice 1992:63-65, also from Geytenbeek & Geytenbeek 1971) and Sharpe 1998 pp.13-14, 16 (held by the project, not a listed work) state that syllables with long vowels are stressed and that a heavy second syllable takes stress away from the initial. There is also a prominence difference among the weight-sensitive sources: Sharpe 1998 says a long vowel elsewhere in the word 'gets the primary stress, and the first syllable is less clear', while Rice 1992 (via StressTyp2) says stress falls on the initial syllable regardless of weight plus every long-vowel syllable, all stresses equally prominent, with the initial destressed only before a heavy second syllable. The catalog's weight-sensitive with a fixed default record follows Rice/StressTyp2; Sharpe 1998 is compatible with it on placement but assigns primary prominence to the long vowel.

sources.note: Sole primary description of Gidabal stress; our classification (weight/CVV, initial default, second-syllable shift, alternate long-vowel shortening) is a database paraphrase of Rice's summary of this book. Reading its phonology/stress pages would convert grade 'quotation carried over second-hand from StressTyp2' to a primary quote and settle whether every non-initial long vowel is stressed (Rice) or weight matters only in the first two syllables (Goedemans 1998 cat. VI 'quantity-sensitive marginal').
